title: Appointees: who was put on which body, by whom, and the money links
question: For commissioners and board members, who holds the power to appoint each seat, who appointed the people sitting now, and did appointees give to the official who appointed them?
finding: The Clerk’s vacancy notices list 943 seats on 100 bodies: 483 filled by the Board, 211 by the Mayor, 20 by the President of the Board and 229 by other officers, jointly or without a printed authority. Of 183 people now holding a Mayor’s seat, the appointing Mayor can be named for 63 (Daniel Lurie 35, London N. Breed 27, Edwin Lee 1). Board files from 2015 record 1,197 approved appointments of a person to a body: 237 by the Mayor, 29 by the President of the Board, 890 by the Board itself and 41 on the nomination of another officer or with none printed. Of 174 mayoral appointees with a rare name, 55 (31.6%) share that name with a donor to the appointing mayor’s committees; 49 (28.2%) share it with a donor to a different mayor’s committees, the comparison that shows how politically active appointees are in general. 24 mayoral appointees are confirmed as donors by a second link. On no body with three or more mayoral appointees do more than half share a name with a donor to the appointing mayor. The President who made the appointment can be named for 27 of 29 presidential appointees; 4 of the 17 with a rare name share it with a donor to that President (5 with a donor to a different President). Of 659 Board appointees with a rare name, 224 (34.0%) share it with a donor to some supervisor.
how: Seats, their holders and the appointing authority are read from the Clerk of the Board’s vacancy notices (dated 2025-01-29 to 2026-10-20); a seat counts as filled when the notice prints a holder who is not marked vacant or holding over. Appointments are the Board’s appointment files of 2015 to 2026, one per file and person, counted when the file passed and its final title does not reject the nominee; the nominating official is the one the file’s own words state. “Mayor” is the person who was Mayor when the file was introduced; the President of the Board is the name on the masthead of the Board’s agendas on both sides of the file’s date. A sitting holder of a Mayor’s seat is tied to the appointing Mayor through the latest Board file for that person and body, or a department’s member page, or the Airport Commission’s printed chronology. Supervisors appointed to regional bodies are left out. Each appointee is looked up by first and last name among donors to the appointing official’s candidate and ballot committees; counts use rare names only (fewer than one other Bay Area resident expected to share the name). An appointee is named as a donor only with a second link: the contribution states the occupation or employer as a commissioner, or its employer is an income source on the appointee’s own Form 700 for the same body. “Declared income” takes the rows of the seat-at-the-table analysis; “business interests” counts appointees with any entry on Form 700 Schedule A-2.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. Mayors appoint people they know and trust, who are often supporters; a contribution of a few hundred dollars is not the price of a seat. A shared name is not a shared identity, which is why only confirmed rows are named, and the comparison with donors to other mayors shows that people who serve on commissions give to campaigns in general. The notices are snapshots with different dates, so a seat may have changed hands since. Commissions the Mayor fills without a Board file (the Airport, Library, Port, Fire, and Recreation and Park Commissions among them) appear only through their own member pages, and rosters before 2025 are not on disk. Advisory bodies whose members file no Form 700 cannot be checked for income or business interests. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
